title: US Driver's Permit: Road Signs and Rules
description: For U.S. permit learners: common sign meanings, right-of-way principles, and safe driving habits. State laws and exceptions differ; consult your current state handbook and verify with current guidelines.

cards.front: What does a red octagonal STOP sign require?
cards.back: Come to a complete stop at the proper stopping point, yield to conflicting traffic and pedestrians, then proceed when safe.

cards.front: What does a downward-pointing triangular YIELD sign mean?
cards.back: Slow and give priority to conflicting traffic or pedestrians; stop if needed to avoid interfering with them.

cards.front: What does a red circle with a white horizontal bar mean?
cards.back: DO NOT ENTER. Do not enter the roadway or ramp from that direction.

cards.front: What does a red rectangular WRONG WAY sign mean?
cards.back: You are traveling against the permitted direction. Stop safely and correct your course without creating another hazard.

cards.front: What does a white rectangular SPEED LIMIT sign show?
cards.back: The legal maximum under the posted conditions. A lower speed may be necessary when conditions are poor.

cards.front: What does a yellow diamond-shaped sign generally indicate?
cards.back: A warning of a condition or hazard ahead, such as a curve or crossing.

cards.front: What do orange road signs generally indicate?
cards.back: Temporary traffic control, commonly for construction or maintenance. Follow the posted directions.

cards.front: What do green guide signs generally provide?
cards.back: Directions, destinations, route information, and distances.

cards.front: What do blue highway service signs generally identify?
cards.back: Motorist services, such as fuel, food, lodging, or medical facilities.

cards.front: What do brown road signs generally identify?
cards.back: Recreational or cultural destinations and facilities.

cards.front: What does a pentagon-shaped school sign indicate?
cards.back: A school area or school crossing. Watch for children and obey any associated speed or crossing controls.

cards.front: What does a round yellow sign with a black X and two R letters warn of?
cards.back: A railroad crossing ahead. Prepare to look and listen for trains and obey crossing controls.

cards.front: What does a railroad crossbuck mark?
cards.back: A railroad crossing. Yield to trains and obey lights, gates, signs, and applicable stop requirements.

cards.front: What does a pennant-shaped NO PASSING ZONE sign indicate?
cards.back: The start of a roadway section where passing is prohibited.

cards.front: What does a ONE WAY sign with an arrow require?
cards.back: Travel only in the direction shown on that roadway.

cards.front: What does a curved left arrow crossed by a red slash mean?
cards.back: No left turn at the indicated location.

cards.front: What does a U-shaped arrow crossed by a red slash mean?
cards.back: No U-turn at the indicated location.

cards.front: What does a NO TURN ON RED sign require?
cards.back: Wait for a signal that permits your turn. Do not turn during the red indication covered by the sign.

cards.front: What does a KEEP RIGHT sign beside an obstruction direct you to do?
cards.back: Pass to the right of the obstruction or divider as indicated.

cards.front: What does a yellow sign showing a lane merging into another warn of?
cards.back: Traffic streams merge ahead. Adjust speed and spacing and be ready to cooperate.

cards.front: What does a LANE ENDS sign require you to prepare for?
cards.back: A lane will end. Plan a safe merge, following local merge controls and road markings.

cards.front: What does a yellow DIVIDED HIGHWAY sign warn of?
cards.back: A median or divider will separate opposing traffic ahead. Stay on the correct side.

cards.front: What does a DIVIDED HIGHWAY ENDS sign warn of?
cards.back: The physical separation of opposing traffic ends ahead. Prepare for two-way traffic on an undivided road.

cards.front: What does a TWO WAY TRAFFIC warning sign indicate?
cards.back: Opposing traffic will share the roadway ahead, often after a one-way or divided section.

cards.front: What does a yellow curve arrow sign warn of?
cards.back: A curve ahead. Adjust speed before entering and remain in your lane.

cards.front: How does an advisory speed plaque differ from a regulatory speed-limit sign?
cards.back: An advisory plaque recommends a speed for a specific condition; a regulatory speed limit establishes a legal maximum. Conditions can require going slower than either.

cards.front: What does a winding-road warning sign indicate?
cards.back: A series of curves ahead. Reduce speed as needed and keep a steady lane position.

cards.front: What does a yellow crossroad symbol warn of?
cards.back: An intersection ahead where cross traffic may enter or cross your path.

cards.front: What does a T-intersection warning sign indicate?
cards.back: The road ahead ends at a crossing road. Prepare to turn and obey the intersection controls.

cards.front: What does a traffic-signal symbol on a warning sign mean?
cards.back: A traffic signal is ahead, possibly not yet easy to see. Be prepared to stop.

cards.front: What does a STOP AHEAD warning sign mean?
cards.back: A stop-controlled intersection is ahead. Begin preparing to stop.

cards.front: What does a yellow pedestrian silhouette sign warn of?
cards.back: A pedestrian crossing or area of pedestrian activity. Watch carefully and yield as required.

cards.front: What does a bicycle symbol on a yellow warning sign mean?
cards.back: Bicyclists may be present or crossing. Give them space and check before turning or changing lanes.

cards.front: What does a deer silhouette warning sign mean?
cards.back: Large animals may cross the road. Scan the roadsides and be ready to slow safely.

cards.front: What does a truck-on-a-slope warning sign indicate?
cards.back: A steep grade ahead. Control speed and select an appropriate gear before descending.

cards.front: What does a slippery-when-wet symbol warn of?
cards.back: Traction may be reduced when the surface is wet. Reduce speed and avoid abrupt maneuvers.

cards.front: What does a NARROW BRIDGE sign warn of?
cards.back: The bridge is narrower than the approaching roadway. Adjust position and speed safely.

cards.front: What does a LOW CLEARANCE sign tell drivers?
cards.back: The available vertical clearance is limited. Know the height of your vehicle and load before proceeding.

cards.front: What does a ROAD CLOSED sign mean?
cards.back: The roadway is closed to through travel at the stated point or section. Follow the authorized detour.

cards.front: What does a DETOUR arrow direct drivers to follow?
cards.back: A temporary alternate route around a closure or restriction.

cards.front: What does a solid red traffic light generally require?
cards.back: Stop at the stop line, before the crosswalk, or before entering the intersection. Remain stopped unless a turn is lawful and safe under local rules.

cards.front: What does a steady yellow traffic light mean?
cards.back: The green interval is ending and red is about to appear. Stop if you can do so safely; do not accelerate to beat the light.

cards.front: What does a circular green traffic light allow?
cards.back: Proceed if the intersection is clear, while yielding to pedestrians and other traffic with priority. Green does not guarantee an unobstructed path.

cards.front: What does a green arrow generally permit?
cards.back: Movement in the arrow's direction during a protected phase, while still checking for pedestrians, vehicles, and other hazards already in the path.

cards.front: What does a flashing red traffic signal mean?
cards.back: Stop completely, then proceed according to stop-sign right-of-way rules when safe.

cards.front: What does a flashing yellow traffic signal mean?
cards.back: Proceed with caution after checking for conflicts. It does not require a stop by itself.

cards.front: What does a flashing yellow left-turn arrow mean?
cards.back: A left turn is permitted after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians; turn only when a safe gap exists.

cards.front: What is the safe default at a red arrow when local rules are unknown?
cards.back: Stop and wait for a permissive signal. Red-arrow turn exceptions differ by jurisdiction; learn the applicable rule.

cards.front: Should you enter an intersection on green if traffic blocks the exit?
cards.back: No. Wait until there is room to clear the intersection without blocking cross traffic or a crosswalk.

cards.front: Whose directions take priority when a traffic officer contradicts a signal?
cards.back: Follow the officer's lawful traffic directions.

cards.front: What should you do at a dark or malfunctioning traffic signal?
cards.back: Slow, prepare to stop, and follow your state's rule and any officer or temporary controls. Do not assume you have priority.

cards.front: What does a pedestrian WALK indication authorize?
cards.back: Pedestrians may begin crossing, while still checking for vehicles. Turning drivers must yield as required.

cards.front: What does a flashing DON'T WALK indication mean for someone already crossing?
cards.back: Continue toward the far side or a safe refuge; drivers must allow the person to finish safely. Rules for starting during countdown phases vary.

cards.front: Where should you stop when a stop line is marked?
cards.back: Before the stop line, keeping the vehicle out of the crosswalk and intersection.

cards.front: Where should you stop at a stop sign without a stop line but with a crosswalk?
cards.back: Before entering the crosswalk, then move forward only as needed and safe to see and yield.

cards.front: Does a rolling stop satisfy a STOP sign?
cards.back: No. The vehicle must fully stop.

cards.front: At a typical all-way stop, who goes first?
cards.back: The driver who stopped first generally proceeds first. When arrivals are simultaneous, yield to the driver on your right; resolve uncertainty cautiously.

cards.front: At an uncontrolled intersection, what common tie-breaking rule applies?
cards.back: When vehicles arrive at about the same time, the driver on the left generally yields to the driver on the right. Local exceptions and signs control.

cards.front: Who generally yields when turning left across oncoming traffic?
cards.back: The left-turning driver yields to oncoming traffic close enough to be a hazard and to pedestrians in the turn path, unless a controlling signal directs otherwise.

cards.front: Who generally yields when entering a road from a driveway?
cards.back: The entering driver yields to road traffic and to pedestrians or bicyclists crossing the driveway.

cards.front: Who generally has priority inside a modern roundabout?
cards.back: Traffic already circulating. Entering drivers yield and follow any signs or lane controls.

cards.front: In which direction does traffic circulate in a U.S. roundabout?
cards.back: Counterclockwise around the central island.

cards.front: How should you choose a lane for a multilane roundabout?
cards.back: Read the approach signs and pavement arrows before entering and select the lane for your intended exit.

cards.front: Should you stop inside a roundabout merely to let another car enter?
cards.back: Generally no. Keep moving with circulating traffic unless a hazard or traffic control requires a stop.

cards.front: What should you do if you miss your freeway exit?
cards.back: Continue to the next safe exit. Never reverse, stop in a travel lane, or cut across the gore area.

cards.front: What is the usual purpose of a freeway acceleration lane?
cards.back: To build an appropriate merging speed and identify a safe gap before joining through traffic.

cards.front: Who must find a safe gap when merging onto a freeway?
cards.back: The entering driver generally yields to traffic already on the freeway, unless traffic controls direct otherwise.

cards.front: When should you normally slow for a freeway exit?
cards.back: Move into the exit lane and then decelerate as conditions permit; follow the exit's advisory speed and traffic conditions.

cards.front: What should you check before changing lanes?
cards.back: Mirrors, the relevant blind spot, surrounding speeds, and a sufficiently large gap. Signal before moving.

cards.front: Does using a turn signal give you right-of-way?
cards.back: No. A signal communicates intent but does not require others to yield.

cards.front: Why should you avoid lingering beside another vehicle?
cards.back: You may be in its blind spot and have less room to respond if it changes lanes.

cards.front: What is the usual function of a two-way center left-turn lane?
cards.back: Preparing for a left turn from either direction. It is not a general travel or passing lane; local entry and distance rules apply.

cards.front: What do yellow centerline markings generally separate?
cards.back: Traffic traveling in opposite directions.

cards.front: What do white lane markings generally separate?
cards.back: Traffic moving in the same direction; white markings also identify road edges and other controls.

cards.front: What does a broken yellow line on your side generally allow?
cards.back: Passing when lawful, visible, and safe. You must still obey signs and restrictions near intersections, hills, or curves.

cards.front: What does a solid yellow line on your side generally prohibit?
cards.back: Crossing it to pass. Some jurisdictions allow crossing for certain turns or obstructions, subject to specific rules.

cards.front: What do double solid yellow centerlines generally prohibit?
cards.back: Passing in either direction. Rules for left turns, driveways, and other exceptions depend on the jurisdiction.

cards.front: What does a broken white lane line generally permit?
cards.back: A lane change when safe and lawful, after checking and signaling.

cards.front: What does a solid white lane line generally communicate?
cards.back: Lane changing is discouraged or restricted depending on the location and local rule. Stay in lane unless movement is permitted and safe.

cards.front: What do double solid white lane lines indicate?
cards.back: Crossing between the separated lanes is prohibited; use a designated opening.

cards.front: What does a diamond symbol in a travel lane commonly indicate?
cards.back: A lane reserved for specified users, such as qualifying high-occupancy vehicles. Read the signs for eligibility and operating times.

cards.front: What do arrows painted in a lane require you to prepare for?
cards.back: The permitted or required movement from that lane. Choose the correct lane before reaching the intersection.

cards.front: What is a freeway gore area?
cards.back: The marked triangular separation between a ramp and the main roadway. Do not use it for a last-second lane change.

cards.front: What does a bicycle sharrow indicate?
cards.back: A shared roadway marking highlighting bicycle travel; it does not create an exclusive bicycle lane.

cards.front: How should you react to a school bus with flashing red lights and an extended stop arm?
cards.back: Stop as your state's law requires and remain stopped until legally permitted to proceed. Divided-road exceptions and opposite-direction rules vary.

cards.front: What do a school bus's flashing yellow lights generally warn of?
cards.back: The bus is preparing to stop. Slow and prepare to stop as required.

cards.front: What should you do for an approaching emergency vehicle using warning lights and a siren?
cards.back: Yield and move out of its path safely, usually toward the right and stopped as local rules direct. Do not block an intersection.

cards.front: What is the purpose of move-over laws?
cards.back: To protect people beside stopped roadside vehicles. Change to a safer lane when required and safe, or slow as the applicable law directs.

cards.front: How should you respond to a flagger in a work zone?
cards.back: Follow the flagger's lawful directions, slow down, and be ready to stop.

cards.front: What should you do when railroad crossing lights flash or a gate lowers?
cards.back: Stop before the crossing as required. Never drive around, under, or through a closing or lowered gate.

cards.front: Should you enter railroad tracks when traffic beyond them is stopped?
cards.back: No. Cross only when there is enough clear space for your entire vehicle beyond the tracks.

cards.front: What should you do if your vehicle stalls on railroad tracks?
cards.back: Get everyone out and away from the tracks immediately. From safety, call the crossing's emergency notification number and emergency services if needed.

cards.front: Why must you check for another train after one passes?
cards.back: A second train may approach on another track or from the opposite direction. Wait for all controls to permit crossing.

cards.front: How should you pass a bicyclist?
cards.back: Wait for a safe, legal opportunity, allow the clearance your state requires and conditions warrant, and return only after fully clearing the rider.

cards.front: Why should you check beside your vehicle before opening a door?
cards.back: A bicyclist, motorcyclist, or other road user may be approaching and could strike the door.

cards.front: How much lane space should you give a motorcycle?
cards.back: Treat it as entitled to a full lane. Do not squeeze alongside it within its lane.

cards.front: Why is extra space useful behind a large truck?
cards.back: It improves your view and gives more time to react; the truck can hide hazards and signals.

cards.front: What are a large truck's no-zones?
cards.back: Large blind areas around the truck where its driver may not see another road user.

cards.front: Why should you avoid passing a truck on the right near an intersection?
cards.back: The truck may swing wide before a right turn and trap a vehicle beside it.

cards.front: What is a safe response to a tailgater?
cards.back: Increase space ahead and, when safe, let the tailgater pass. Avoid brake-checking or confrontation.

cards.front: How should following distance change in rain or poor visibility?
cards.back: Increase it. Reduced traction or visibility leaves less margin for braking and hazard detection.

cards.front: Why is a posted speed limit not always a safe speed?
cards.back: It does not account for every moment's weather, visibility, surface, traffic, or vehicle condition.

cards.front: What should you do before a sharp curve?
cards.back: Reduce speed before entering, then steer smoothly and avoid abrupt braking within the curve.

cards.front: What is hydroplaning?
cards.back: Loss of tire contact with the road as tires ride on water, reducing steering and braking control.

cards.front: What should you do if the vehicle begins hydroplaning?
cards.back: Ease off the accelerator, keep steering smooth, and avoid sudden braking or sharp turns while traction returns.

cards.front: Which headlights are usually better in fog?
cards.back: Low beams. High beams can reflect from droplets and increase glare.

cards.front: What should you do if oncoming headlights cause glare?
cards.back: Avoid staring into them; use the right road edge as a guide while maintaining awareness and reducing speed if needed.

cards.front: What does overdriving your headlights mean?
cards.back: Traveling so fast that your stopping distance exceeds the road distance illuminated ahead.

cards.front: Why is using cruise control in very slippery conditions risky?
cards.back: Automatic speed control may respond poorly when traction changes; maintain direct control and follow the vehicle manual.

cards.front: What should you do if you become sleepy while driving?
cards.back: Leave the roadway at a safe place and rest or arrange another driver. Opening a window does not reliably restore alertness.

cards.front: Does coffee make an impaired driver sober?
cards.back: No. Caffeine does not remove alcohol or restore safe driving ability; only time reduces the body's alcohol burden.

cards.front: Can prescription or nonprescription medicine impair driving?
cards.back: Yes. Follow warnings and professional instructions, and do not drive if the medicine impairs alertness, vision, or coordination.

cards.front: Why is texting dangerous even during a familiar trip?
cards.back: It takes visual, manual, and mental attention away from driving; hazards can develop within seconds.

cards.front: What should you do before using a phone for a nonurgent task?
cards.back: Park safely in a lawful place before handling the task. Follow local device-use restrictions.

cards.front: What should occupants do with seat belts before moving?
cards.back: Use properly fitted seat belts in every seating position; secure children in the legally appropriate restraint.

cards.front: Why must child-restraint requirements be checked locally?
cards.back: Required ages, sizes, seating positions, and restraint types vary by jurisdiction; follow current law and the restraint manufacturer's instructions.

cards.front: How should loose cargo be handled before driving?
cards.back: Secure it so it cannot shift, strike occupants, block visibility, or fall onto the road.

cards.front: Why should you never drive into floodwater covering a road?
cards.back: Depth, current, and road damage may be hidden; even apparently shallow water can disable or move a vehicle. Turn around safely.

cards.front: What should you do after a collision involving possible injury?
cards.back: Stop safely, prevent further danger where possible, summon emergency help, and follow local duties to assist, exchange information, and report.

cards.front: Why should you consult your own state's current driver's handbook?
cards.back: Permit exams and enforceable details vary by state. This deck covers shared principles, not every local rule or exception.
